utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the answer. Could the witness please be asked to speak closer to the microphone too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born? The interpreters didn't get the answer, so if you could just repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gradacac is in Bosnia and Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's in the municipality of Samac [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you complete your education?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Samac. I completed my primary and secondary school in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one intervention to the transcript. First on, it is on page 49, answer on the line 9. It's not properly recorded. It's the neighbouring municipality of -- to Samac. This is what the witness said. Gradacac is actually not in the municipality of Samac and the witness has just said it's a neighbouring municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, can he give the name of the municipality? That would be much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buzakovic, you've told us that you were born in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Is Gradacac in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Gradacac a municipality neighbouring on the municipality of Samac in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a post official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live up to the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you reside now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the war, between 1992 and 1995, did you stay in Samac the whole time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Gornji Milanovac, in 1985 and 1986, in Gorjni Milanovac and then I got a transfer to Kikanda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please state your ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party or organisation? Are you now a member of any party or organisation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of any party nor am I a member of any party today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the 4th Detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you became a member of the 4th Detachment. You were given weapons.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any position in the detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was just a common soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on to events on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Where were you and what did you do on the 16th and 17th -- on the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1992, I was working at a local pub or cafe. The name of the cafe was Monika [as interpreted]. It was in the centre of town. I worked until evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you close down?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: We shut at half past 9.00 or 10.00. That was unusually early.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you shut that early?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Our people usually stay outside in the cafes very late, 11.00, midnight. But that evening there was no one about town because the cafe is plumb in the centre of town. But there were no people walking around. There were no clients, patrons, so there was no need for me to stay open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... to my learned friend. I think that we heard that the name of the cafe was Monca, like Italian town, Monca. It's on line 13, page 51. In the transcript we have "Monika." So maybe it might be importance. So I don't know if it's important for my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, was the name of the cafe Monca, as Mr. Pantelic says? Yes. That will be corrected. You proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the name of the cafe.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Monca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That night, the 17th of April, did anything out of the ordinary happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. I came home as usual. I had dinner. I went to bed at some point. During the night, about 3.00 hours in the morning we were awakened by sounds of shooting, my mother and I, from the eastern part of the town and there was a powerful explosion about 3.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a suggestion from my colleague here. You're talking about a part of the night of the 17th in the morning hours. That's when you heard those things.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the eastern part of town. Can you please briefly describe what do you mean do you mean by the eastern part of Samac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's towards the silo, that's the general direction of the memorial centre, the SUP, Donja Mahala, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard shooting, when you heard the explosions, what happened at your building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Outside in the hall of the building we heard commotion, we heard people talking, so I opened the door and at the entrance to the building I noticed all my neighbours. I noticed quite many members of the 4th Battalion [as interpreted] who were in the detachment with me, so we exchanged comments as to what was going on and what might happen. We didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that in the hall you noticed many members of the 4th Battalion standing there -- 4th Detachment, rather, were those your neighbours who lived in the same building, the same entrance and they were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they, too, leave their flats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: We were neighbours. We all left our flats and came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Did you go anywhere? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't go anywhere. We just stayed in our homes. We agreed as neighbours not to allow any unknown persons into the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to use the phone to find out what was happening?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, a number of times, but the phone lines were down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the phone lines were down, and you couldn't find out what was happening.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, the phone lines were down. We couldn't find out what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened the next morning with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: About 8.00 in the morning I was surprised because the phone rang, and it was a relative of mine calling and he said that some police had taken the eastern part of the town and he didn't really have any reliable information about what had happened, so I just stayed home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report to the command of the 4th Detachment when the phone started working again?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what it was about. After I talked to my relative, the phone rang, and on the other end of the line there was someone from the command telling me to report with full combat kit to the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: The SIT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your neighbours who were also members of the 4th Detachment, did they come with you then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them. Some of them, depending on how they were called up and when they reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these neighbours of yours that you referred to, that you said were members of the 4th Detachment from your building and from that particular part of the building where your flat was, were there only ethnic Serbs or were there Muslims, Croats, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a multi-ethnic unit. There were some members of this unit who were Muslims. And I know that personally because they were my neighbours. They were Muslims and Croats. It was multi-ethnic. Truth to tell, the majority were Serbs but there were quite a few Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question pertained to the part of the building where you lived. Could you remember the Muslims who were members of the 4th Detachment who were your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atic. We called him Hamko. I don't know what his real name was. There was a Sejhapovic [phoen], I think. Was his first name Muhamed, or whatever, I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You came to the command and what did you find at the command of the 4th Detachment of the SIT building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment I came, there were about 20 soldiers there, or rather -- well, about 20 members of the 4th Detachment. Some people were in uniform, some people were in jackets. There were about 20 of them there. And then the number went up as time went by. It was about 9.00 or 9.30, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So members of the 4th Detachment came and they were there in front of the command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Commander Antic, did he take you then to have a combat task carried out, namely to take the outskirts of the town of Samac, or rather, the embankment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he took us to the embankment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay at the embankment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: At that embankment we stayed there all night, until the morning. I think it was about 5.30 or 6.00 in the morning when a new shift came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the evening of the 17th, did you get some white ribbons so that you could be distinguished?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about dusk when they brought us white ribbons. I had a uniform. I wore a uniform, and I put that white ribbon on my left epaulette and people who did not have uniform and who were wearing jackets put them on their left upper arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a while ago that you stayed until 5.30 or 6.00. So that is already the 18th, at 5.30 or 6.00 you left these positions. Were you replaced by another shift?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they told us that we could go home to get a bit of rest and not to go anywhere from home, that we should await further activities and further obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you called to the command of the 4th Detachment again that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, around 9.00, 9.30, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get some new tasks there, some new orders?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: We were given new tasks and new orders. We were told that we should go to collect weapons in the 4th quarter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given some orders and instructions related to the collection of weapons in the 4th quarter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you were told.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: The procedure was explained to us, also how we should address citizens and when we walk into yards and houses that we should knock or ring the bell, not to break into any homes, not to ask anyone for anything in a violent manner, that we should act in a neighbouring fashion, that is to say, no force, no compulsion, no orders, nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "in this neighbourly fashion," does that mean that citizens were supposed to act in a voluntary fashion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were in this one group that was supposed to carry out this task?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: In my group, there were about ten of us, nine or ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did you wear?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had an olive-grey uniform on, and it was a bit rainy and there was even a bit of sleet, so I had some tarpaulin over the uniform. Other people did not even have a uniform. They were wearing civilian clothes. So we were not all in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you escorted by an armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were escorted by an armoured combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain this, what an armoured combat vehicle is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: An armoured combat vehicle, an ACV - in B/C/S, BOV - is a vehicle that has a turret with three barrels with three 20-millimetre guns, that is, anti-aircraft weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So an ACV is a vehicle with rubber wheels and it has a turret with three barrels.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: With three barrels, three guns. That's what we say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you set out. Which street did you take?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we started out from the SIT and we took the former street of Kardelj. Now it is called the street of Car Dusan. And we went left and right down the street in the direction of the post office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This armoured combat vehicle, this ACV, as you call it, did it move behind you, in front of you, together with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was behind us. It was behind us. And the distance was about 15, 20, or 30 metres. It depended how much it would stay behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the position of these guns?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: The guns were raised in relation to us, because that is what had been agreed upon because the guns were not to be supposed to -- they were not supposed to be pointed in our direction, and that is why they were raised further up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Something did not enter the transcript. When you said why the guns were not raised, so could you repeat that. Why were the guns not raised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: The ACV has three guns and the guns, the barrels, can be put down, and this -- and it's about 2 and a half or 3 metres up and then they can be down or they can be taken up at an angle of up to 90 degrees. So they were not pointed at us at all, so that we would not be hurt in any way, even accidentally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause. The interpreters could not catch this because both speakers were speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, do pause. Don't overlap the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Just on this question of the guns. I wonder, Mr. Buzakovic, you say the guns were up on the combat vehicle, and you've just mentioned they could be sort of halfway up or at 90 degrees. Do you recall whether they were fully up at 90 degrees, so they were just pointing up into the sky, not pointing at anyone, not pointing at you, not pointing at any civilians on the street and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I have to correct you. These are not rifles. These are barrels, guns, on a turret, and they can be down, lower down, but they can go up, up to 90 degrees. So they were raised. They were quite high up in relation to us. Not a 90-degree angle but in that direction. So they could not really fire at us or at any buildings or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, Mr. Buzakovic, I didn't say "rifles." I did say "guns." Obviously a translation into B/C/S problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But the interpretation we heard said "rifles," and that is why this came as an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this combat vehicle, did it stop every now and then while you were collecting weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle was not moving all the time. It would stop every now and then. It would stop and wait, because usually my group, approximately ten people, three of us would usually walk into the yard, knock at the door. So usually it would be three of us in front of a house and then the other three would be in front of another house, and then the other three would be in front of a third house, and then we would collect weapons and throw them into the combat vehicle and that is why it was that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us now clarify one matter: So this was not a tank.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this task was being carried out, did you make any exceptions when you came to various houses, apartment buildings, et cetera, or did you go to all doors of buildings and apartments?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: When we set out from the command of the 4th Detachment, we were told that we should go into every house, every yard, every apartment, indiscriminately. Not to enter the premises but to knock at the door. So we did not make any distinctions, regardless of whether it was a Serb, Muslim, or Croat house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any situations when citizens were already waiting for you in their yards and handing over weapons to you and that you didn't even have to enter the yards, let alone the houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such situations. There were also people who were frightened. And then, on the other hand, there were people who even gave us coffee and cigarettes. As a matter of fact, even a little brandy or two. And there were situations when we gave people cigarettes as well, because there were situations when people would not leave their houses, so they couldn't even buy their own cigarettes. So generally speaking, the cooperation was exceptionally good between us and the citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I hope you are watching your time. Yes. You have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went into the street of Pero Bosic at one point, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Esad Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us what happened on that day when you came to the house of Esad Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: My group, since this was the second house in this street -- or rather, in this yard there are two houses. We entered this yard. I, Fadil Topcagic, and there was another soldier with us, Nenad. Nenad was his first name. Nenad was his first name, at any rate. In the first house in this yard we knocked at the door and nobody answered and we went further into the yard, and then I walked up a few steps and I knocked at the door and Esad Dagovic, nicknamed Ekac, came out. The usual procedure: Hello, hello. Esad, do you have any weapons? And he said to me that he had a pistol and that he had a proper permit for it. I said to him that he should bring his pistol and I asked him, "Do you have any military weapons, army weapons?" And the door was a bit ajar and I think his mother was there behind the door, peeking through, his mother and his brother, and he told me that I should follow him. I followed him. He walked into the basement. And in the corner of the basement, underneath the coal that was there - so this was at the very end of the basement - he dug through the coal a bit and -- now, in some cloth there was an automatic rifle with one clip on it, one clip of ammunition on it, and there were also two hand grenades there wrapped in that cloth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a Kalashnikov rifle?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got out of the basement, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Even in the basement he said to me, "Goran --" perhaps I can even quote him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: "I swear by my mother that I did not shoot from these weapons." I personally was not interested in this, but he went out and he cocked the rifle and opened it and he -- it was obvious that the weapons had not been fired from, either the rifle or the pistol. And I asked him, because an automatic rifle is usually issued in -- as part of combat equipment. I asked him, "Ekac, do you have this combat set with more clips of ammunition?" "No," he said. "That's the only thing I had. No, nothing." So that was it. "Bye, bye." And then we went further. And I put his weapons into the ACV that was following us. But we put all these weapons in the ACV and then we would proceed further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, what about Mr. Simo Zaric and Mr. Miroslav Tadic? At that moment, were they ever together with you? Were they ever in this group of soldiers that was collecting weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a single moment did I -- I didn't notice them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them that day at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see them that day at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you complete this action?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime earlier in the evening. I don't know. About 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Regular activities. Well, then they told us that we could go home and that we should be ready to go to the outskirts of town to take over from these people who were at the embankment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spent the entire day as a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the entire day as a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further answers [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't make much sense here on page 63. "So you spent the entire day as a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska." First of all, it was not the day. It was a war that Mr. Pisarevic was referring to, because at that time the Army of Republika Srpska didn't even exist. It was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the pace was extreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that was the problem. It was too fast. Can you ask the last question again, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from 1992 until the end of the war, 1995, you were a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel? Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These orders you received on the morning when you went searching for weapons, who gave you those orders?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: We received orders from the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Antic, and later on from the commander of my unit, my company, Rajko Dragic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that Antic personally gave the assembled soldiers such as yourself the orders as to what to do in weapons collection? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Antic say that you, that is, the soldiers in the 4th Detachment, were not to enter people's houses? Was that one of the orders he gave you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that weapons were to be collected in such a way that citizens would bring their weapons outside to a collection point in their own garden and then members of the detachment were to collect them? Is that what Antic said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- is it true that Antic sternly warned all you collected soldiers against entering people's houses in an arbitrary manner? Is it true that he ordered -- that he said that to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Antic said to you that nothing was to be seized but weapons of a military origin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: We were looking for weapons of military origin. However, there were people who turned over --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I asked. I asked you what Antic said. Please listen to the question. Is it true that Antic said to you when giving you those orders that nothing was to be seized but weapons collected of a military origin? Is that what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: He said that we should take all the weapons that people would turn over, but we were originally looking for weapons of military origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't say that you were only to take weapons of military origin; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: It is my submission that he told us that he -- that we should take weapons of military origin and any other weapons being turned over. People were turning over weapons. They were too scared to keep those weapons at home. Whether it was military weapons or some other weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness said at the end, the witness was talking about illegal weapons, and the Prosecutor is talking about military weapons. So illegal weapons is a somewhat broader concept. So if the Prosecutor could please refer to illegal weapons or illegally owned weapons, because those are not necessarily weapons of military origin. So we're talking about weapons that people should not be allowed to keep at home without proper permit, and that's exactly what the witness said. So in order to keep the Prosecutor from further confusing the witness, maybe we should be using the term "illegal weapons," or rather, "illegally owned weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. I'm quoting evidence of this witness. I'm quoting it from the transcript. For my friend's benefit, page T17O30 [as said].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take you back to my question, sir. I'm asking you about what Antic said in relation to the collection of weapons. Is it true -- I withdraw that. Did he say to you that only weapons of military origin were to be collected?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: He told us to collect weapons of military origin and whatever weapons the citizens were willing to hand over on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zaric, who's called you to give evidence here, gave a statement to the Prosecution in 1998 in which he said the orders were not to go into people's houses. That's P141 ter at pages 18 to 19, for my friend's benefit. Do you agree with that statement, that the orders were not to go into people's houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about Mr. Zaric's statement. I'm not sure who he gave this statement to. What I do know, however, is that we did not enter houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just told you. It was to the Prosecution. I wasn't asking you about that. I was asking you about what he said. In his statement to the Prosecution, he said "we were not to enter houses," period, "not to enter houses."

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Except if someone invited us. And I was invited into the basement of that specific house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you a moment ago, sir, about what Antic said, you said nothing about except if people invite you into the house, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew those people there personally. We were ordered not to use force to get into houses, no breaking and entering, no banging on the door, no threatening people in order to get into their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're now saying, are you, that the orders Antic gave were that you could enter houses if people allowed you to come in and search them? Is that what you're saying now, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: We understood Mr. Antic's order, but Mr. Antic did not know that I knew certain people in town very well and that they indeed knew me well. It was up to me. So I came into another house. It was a neighbour of mine. And she offered me coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did Antic say that you could interpret these orders not to enter houses as if people invited us in to the house, we could search if we wanted to? Did he tell you you could interpret his orders in any way that you chose?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Antic ordered us not to enter any houses, not to enter by force, no breaking in, no use of force. Everything had to be done on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The situation was, sir, on this particular day there were nine or ten armed soldiers, some in uniform, some not, carrying Kalashnikovs, accompanied by a -- an ACV or BOV with three barrels pointing in different directions, knocking on people's doors looking for weapons. That's your evidence, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mind you, my group contained about ten soldiers, so my group, the ten of us, were there. And there were other groups there. But I'm only talking about my group. We were about ten people in the group, and we went from house to house indiscriminately. We knocked on people's doors. Whoever was at home would open. Many people were simply not home. That's what the situation was like. And it had been for quite some time. There was something in the air, that something just wasn't quite right, and many people from the country lived in the town and they would just simply leave town for the weekend, go away. We were walking and the barrels were raised up in the air for our safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't think this might be intimidating to people whose doors you were knocking on, seeing nine or ten armed soldiers with the Kalashnikovs outside in the street accompanied by a -- an APC -- sorry, ACV BOV with three barrels? That wouldn't be intimidating to the citizens of Bosanski Samac whose doors you're knocking on, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not all ten of us were knocking. We usually went in groups of three. Intimidating? Well, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say that. I said nine or ten soldiers outside. I didn't say nine or ten were knocking on the door. Please concentrate on what I said. Nine or ten soldiers in the vicinity, outside in the street, while you or others were knocking on the door accompanied by an armoured vehicle with three barrels. Are you saying people didn't find that intimidating, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course they were intimidated, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not supposed to intimidate anyone. Now, how people felt at the moment, I really can't say. And there were always three of us in a yard at any given point in time because the other group of three would already have moved ahead to a different house, which was 50 metres further down the street. And the ACV was sometimes as much as 30, 40, or 50 metres behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric, who you both know seated over there, were given the task of supervising the collection of weapons immediately after the Serb takeover, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the job of supervising entailed them going from groups of soldiers to groups of soldiers to ensure they were going about their task in the designated and ordered way, didn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a -- I can't see a question. I think that's rather the suggestion of an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sir, it is. That's right. They were given the job of supervising. There were different groups going round the town, knocking on doors looking for weapons. Supervision meant that they went to the different groups to make sure they were doing their job, didn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them on that particular day at all. Maybe they were supposed to be doing that, but I didn't see them on that day or the previous day, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that because you were too busy inside people's houses searching for weapons, you didn't notice them going from group to group supervising your activities, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Calling for speculation. I really don't believe what might be the reason why he didn't say them. There is also an explanation that maybe they weren't there also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I asked him if the reason was because he was inside searching for weapons. It's fairly specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the reason you didn't see them -- see them supervising you carrying out your task because you were inside houses searching for weapons or having cups of coffee or drinking brandy or providing cigarettes to the citizens of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. When we came to people's homes, to the yards, we would look around every time, checking for traps because people were armed and we were trying to keep our own men from getting killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm asking you about the reason why you may not have seen them if they were doing their job properly. Was it possibly because you were indoors either searching for weapons or coffee, brandy, or cigarette -- cigarette provision to the citizens of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how they went about their own work. I only know that on that particular day I myself did not see anywhere, not in the yards, not behind us, I didn't see them. Not that I didn't see them because I was having coffee in someone else's house or was drinking alcohol and giving people cigarettes. I didn't see them for the simple fact that they just weren't there. So that's my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. But given that Antic's orders were not to enter people's houses and only to seize weapons of a military origin, if Tadic or Zaric acting under those orders had seen you in someone's house, their job as the supervising officers would have been to pull you out of the houses, wouldn't it, if they were doing their job properly? Wouldn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I don't think the witness can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He's answered that they were supervising him. The orders were not to enter people's houses. My question is based upon that, if they, as a the supervising officers of the search had been doing their job properly, had people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- people's houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They should have pulled them out and Zaric had seen it or Tadic had seen it or known about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can't say what they could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What they should have done based on Antic's [Realtime transcript read in error "Tadic's"] orders, not what they could have done. The orders are not to enter houses. The supervising officers should have pulled the soldiers out if they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I don't think the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buzakovic, by that stage, of course, there were already tanks in Bosanski Samac, weren't there? By the time you were doing your door-to-door searches for weapons, there were already several tanks in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have exactly what my learned friend and colleague from the Prosecution said. I think my colleague has misspoken on page 71, line 9. I think he was supposed to say on Tadic's orders. I think he meant on Antic's orders, actually, not on Tadic's orders. So I would like to see a correction there, because we never heard that Tadic had actually given any orders, unless the Prosecutor actually meant what he said. But I think the meaning was Antic's orders, page 71, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly. If I said "Tadic," it was completely inadvertent. I thought I said "Antic," but it says "Tadic." There. That can be certainly clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was about tanks. By the time you were searching -- doing your door-to-door searches, there were already several tanks in Bosanski Samac, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not in our vicinity. The whole district, no, there were no tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the tanks arrive, sir? These two tanks, when did they come, in relation to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about tanks that I never saw. I don't know that there were two tanks there. There were certainly no tanks near where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see any tanks in Bosanski Samac in the days immediately after the takeover on the 17th of April, 1992; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's precisely what I'm saying. After the takeover, I did not see any tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in charge of the group that was going -- the nine or ten soldiers doing the door-to-door searches for weapons, or was someone else in charge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not in charge of the group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubo Simic was in charge of my group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ljubo Simic have any -- were you given any indication of people you should look for, of houses you should go to looking for weapons, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't told to look for any specific people, and we searched houses indiscriminately, one by one. No distinctions made. And we weren't looking for any of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you just said you searched houses indiscriminately, what you meant is you went into houses searching, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't actually say that we searched houses. We'd go as far as the door and ask about weapons. When I say "ask," I don't mean that I actually searched any houses. We would approach the person who the house belonged to, say, "Hello, hello. Do you happen to have any weapons in the house; yes or no?" We did not search houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago -- and I'm just reading from your answer, no, we weren't told to look for any specific people and we "searched houses indiscriminately one by one." That's what I've got in front of me here. What did you mean -- I'm sorry, when you said "we searched houses indiscriminately," you meant you went into houses looking for weapons, didn't you, sir? That's what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness has already explained, Mr. Re. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, his answer was "asked," not searched. He used the word "searched." I asked him what he meant by searched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He answered. If you look at the answer in 73, 12, he explained what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, there's now two answers on the transcript. One is we searched houses, and the other one is we didn't search houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, he did explain. Mr. Re, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, when you -- when you went with the 4th Detachment searching, were any of the members of the specials, the people who had come into the district, were they on your patrol searching house to house?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only members of the 4th Detachment were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this search of Mr. Dagovic's house, when you went to his cellar, did you videotape this search, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I entered because I was invited by him. I didn't do the searching myself. He did the searching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Did you videotape it? Did you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't tape it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone videotape it, sir; yes or no? Answer that one.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took weapons from his house, did you give him a receipt for them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take a photograph of the weapons that you say you took from his house or did anyone to your knowledge take a photograph of these weapons you say were seized from his house with his consent?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or anyone else write a report on the seizure of weapons from his house?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pistol of course wasn't a weapon of military origin, was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: The pistol --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pistol, sir. Was it a Kalashnikov or an -- an RPG or a rifle? It was a pistol for which he had a permit, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: A pistol is also part of military weaponry, 7.62 millimetres. That's a military weapon. And I didn't see a permit there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him for the permit, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't ask to see it. He told me himself that he had a pistol, which he brought himself and turned it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had a pistol. He told you he had a permit for it. You didn't ask for the permit. You didn't see the permit. But you just took it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he never got it back, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was stolen from him, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened later, whether it was returned to him or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stole the weapon from him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, that's not fair to this witness. He has explained -- and it's not fair to be suggesting that he stole from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the searches were completed, sir, the JNA or the 4th Detachment, you said that there was -- there were various duties which it performed. Did the 4th Detachment or a group of which you were a part, take part in guarding any of the vital facilities in the town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war or -- I don't think I understood your question. Can you please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And Mr. Re, you should be winding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover, sir, did the 4th Detachment guard facilities in the town, such as the SUP, the MUP, the TO, the post office, the schools, the river banks, the silos, the waterworks, the municipal buildings, the radio station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not how it was. We were along the perimeter of the town. We were securing the perimeter. But we were not inside the town, actually. And we did not provide security for any of the facilities inside the town; only the perimeter, the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I finally want to suggest to you that you just barged into Esad Dagovic's house, went to his cellar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say. That's your submission. I never said this. I did not barge into anyone's house or into anyone's basement. He actually invited me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that armed soldiers, of which you were a group, pointed their weapons at him saying, "Surrender your weapons. Surrender your weapons."

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No way. Not a chance. That's not how it was. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions. Re-examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You and your group, did you search any house while you were carrying out your task in the 4th quarter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you knew that people knew that people were armed. Were you afraid as you were going down the street that somebody would shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this require some kind of additional caution in view of the situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We had no idea who could start shooting at us at any given point in time. We were there like moving targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or do you think that the citizens of Samac were afraid when a group of 100 Muslims in the centre of town walked around?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and demonstrated with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, you can't ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw. I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this voluntary collection was actually amnesty for citizens --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I mean, Mr. Pisarevic has a habit of asking leading questions in re-examination too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You raised the issue whether some kind of certificates were given in relation to the weapons that were taken away. I'm just trying to say that at that time, in the time of war, it was not advisable and that would not be the effect of voluntary surrender of weapons if people had to sign documents and whatever. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, you are not supposed to give evidence. The witness could have explained that, if there were any reasons why they didn't give certificates, but he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, actually, it was a receipt that was being asked about, not a certificate. That has a slightly different connotation, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely my objective, when I tried to put this question about amnesty. You see, in our part of the world "amnesty" has a meaning of its own. Very often a state would proclaim amnesty so that people could legalise their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in order to prevent anyone from knowing who were the people who had illegal weapons, was that the reason why they were not given certificates, these people whose weapons were collected?

utterances.speaker: GORAN BUZAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Every question that Mr. Pisarevic has asked is either cross-examination or leading. He just can't do it. He's been here long enough to know that's not the way the Rules of Evidence work in this Tribunal. He can ask anything, who, what, where, how, when that arises out of cross-examination, but not in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, you're suggesting answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buzakovic, for giving evidence. You are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Re did say that he wanted to make -- the Trial Chamber was informed that you wanted to make further submissions on the issue of the statement regarding, I think, Kemal Bobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Is it the appropriate time now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We haven't got another witness, have we? Yes. So we can go ahead. Or if you're -- are you collecting your papers? Then we can have Mr. Pantelic in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, that's just -- my suggestion was the same, to leave additional time for my learned friend to collect papers. Your Honour, very briefly, it is the issue with regard to the exhibit D163/1 ID. In fact, that was the -- one of the 92 bis statements of our witnesses. Namely, it is Mr. Simic, Cedomir. And I would kindly ask for some guidance and some alliance from this Honourable Trial Chamber. According to your ruling, it was made on 28 February this year, you said that -- actually the Trial Chamber ruled that the statement in Exhibit D163/1 ID will be on viva voce restricted to matters that is in paragraph 20, and then you wrote about the time limits, et cetera. After carefully reviewing this statement, the Defence is of the opinion that frankly all the statements is dealing with on some cumulative or repetitive way, in fact, about the work of executive board, about the issues that we already covered on many occasions with many witnesses in our case. I mean, I'm speaking on behalf of Defence of Mr. Blagoje Simic. So in order to speed up proceedings, the Defence of Blagoje Simic will not call this witness here. So there are several possibilities. Maybe we could strike paragraph 20 in its totality or we could strike all these statements as exhibits. So it's up to the Trial Chamber, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, it's up to you. If you're saying you wish to withdraw that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- and you don't wish to call him, it's up to you to say so. It's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, that would be the position of the Defence of Blagoje Simic, because there are many repetitive issues here and we shall -- we shall withdraw this statement from the exhibits, because as I said, he repeated speaking about the same issues that the other witnesses are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will consider that and give its ruling in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My application is the following: Yesterday I sought to move into evidence a portion of the statement of Mr. Kemal Bobic dated the 3rd of April, 1998. It's not in evidence at the moment, but for the purposes of the -- my application, can I hand a copy of the relevant portion to Your Honours for the purposes of ruling on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First describe it. What is it discussing and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can read it to Your Honour. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And who recorded it and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a witness statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, interviewers Bernard O'Donnell and Paul Basham, on the 3rd of April, 1998, signed with a declaration. And it's a sentence -- it's a sentence I -- a line I read to the witness, Mr. Sejdic, yesterday, when Your Honours permitted me to reopen for that one question, which would only -- only as to credibility. And the portion is simply this: "On the 17th of April, 1992 I was informed by police from Bosanski Samac police station that I should not leave the area of my house and that I should report to the police station twice a day, either by phone or in person. I asked a policeman named Naser Sejdic, who had ordered this -- sorry, who had ordered this not who had ordered it, wrong emphasis -- and I was told that it was Simo Zaric. Simo Zaric was a security officer in the 4th Detachment of the JNA." That's the portion of the statement which I would seek to tender into evidence only on the issue of Mr. Sejdic's credibility. Now, the reason why I do this, and I know Your Honours will be saying what about 92 bis and a statement complying with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. You finish your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The reason for this application now is that - and I raised this during my objection to the Defence leading evidence relating to the arrest of Mr. Bobic on the -- I think it was the 23rd of May, 1992 - because the Defence had not, pursuant to Rule 90(H)(ii) put a contrary case to either Ediba Bobic or Kemal Bobic when the two gave evidence as to Mr. Bobic's arrest. At no time during the cross-examination did the Defence suggest to either of those witnesses that they were, A, mistaken or, B, untruthful about Mr. Sejdic actually arresting Mr. Bobic, coming to the house and arresting him, or C, that it was a third person who Mr. Sejdic gave evidence of yesterday. I think the name was Cedo [phoen] or something like that, who actually was on the patrol who arrested him. The statement of Mr. Bobic and Mrs. Bobic was served on the Defence many years ago and the Defence had the statement of Mr. Bobic and clearly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Kemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Kemal Bobic, which was shown by Mr. Pisarevic in re-examination -- sorry, in cross-examination at page -- transcript T11502, reading a passage of the statement to the witness. That's Mr. Bobic. The passage which he read was -- was a different passage of the statement, but he -- sorry, it was T11501 to 502. But before that, he actually clarified with the witness, Mr. Kemal Bobic, who Naser Sejdic was saying, "A few questions. This Naser, as a matter of fact, is policeman Naser Sejdic, called Cakar, C-a-k-a-r; is that right?" "Yes." Question: "And in that incident -- in an incident you mentioned happened on the 23rd of May, isn't it?" "Yes." He then -- Mr. Pisarevic then read a passage of the statement. The point of which was in the statement, the passage relating to the arrest, the witness had not said I was -- "I'm arresting you on Simo Zaric's orders." The explanation the witness then gave was, "Well, the Prosecutor didn't ask me all those questions I asked" or -- his explanation was, "Did I read correctly what's written here?" That's T11052. "That is correct, Mr. Bobic? Is that your statement?" "It is." Question: "But Mr. Bobic, you still stand by the statement which you gave on the 3rd of April, 1998 to the investigators of the OTP, of The Hague Tribunal?" Answer: "You mean this statement?" He's meaning the statement -- the 4th of April. Question: "Yes." Answer: "I do stand by it. Why, this is all correct." Question: "It is all correct." Answer: "Yes, it is. If you want me to help somebody with something, that's fine with me." And then it goes on. He asks -- and then it -- and that is basically the extent of any cross-examination, which suggests anything other than what we heard from Mr. Sejdic yesterday. Now, on re-examination, the Prosecution didn't take Mr. Bobic to the earlier portion where he mentioned Mr. Zaric's name, and there's a perfectly obvious explanation for that just from reading the transcript, and that is there would appear to have been no reason to do so because the arrest and the circumstances never -- that is, that Mr. Sejdic actually arrested Mr. Bobic, as opposed to whether he said Mr. Zaric ordered you do so, which is simply never put into question. And the Prosecution, until two days ago, had no idea that there was any challenge to the fact that Mr. Sejdic had arrested Mr. Bobic on Mr. Bobic's and Mrs. Bobic's then unchallenged testimony. So there was simply no reason for the Prosecution to re-examine that portion of the statement in, as they would have been entitled to, back in July 2002 when the evidence was given. The Prosecution is hampered or hamstrung on the issue of credibility with Mr. Sejdic because we were not able to put that -- or ask Mr. Bobic about that statement. However, Mr. Pisarevic asked him whether the statement, that is, the 4th of April, 1998, was correct, and he said it was in its entirety, meaning he has given -- he has sworn on oath correctness of the statement the portion of which I am moving to tender into evidence. Now, the basis of tender is only as to the credibility of Mr. Sejdic. It's not as to whether Mr. Zaric actually spoke those words, because that is hearsay and the Prosecution would not be at this stage wanting to use those words against him as secondhand hearsay. It goes only as to Mr. Sejdic saying to the witness, Mr. Bobic, "Zaric told me to do something." Now, whether Zaric did or not is a different matter. The question is whether he said that Zaric had done so at some point, and it's a very narrow issue of -- of admission into evidence. It's not related to the truth of whether Mr. Zaric actually said that to Mr. Sejdic. So those are my submissions. The only other alternative the Prosecution would have that I could see would be to obtain a 92 bis statement from Mr. Bobic to tender in rebuttal as to that particular portion. But in my submission, as he's already testified, sworn on earth to its veracity, that should not be necessary. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why -- yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will give a very brief submission to that, to the submission of my learned colleague. The Defence cross-examined this witness. And such a problem never raised. The truth is that it was the first time here that Mr. Bobic mentioned that Mr. -- that he heard that Mr. Zaric ordered to Mr. Sejdic, who was also a witness here, to arrest allegedly Mr. Bobic. That was actually the first time that we heard this information, this piece of information. Of course we cannot know what each and every witness would say before this Tribunal when he comes to testify here. Some things appear suddenly during proofing with witnesses. And in such a case, the Defence and the Prosecution as well need to check the truthness of such an information. We heard it from the witness. Then we addressed to our investigators in the field. They tried to reach Mr. Sejdic and everything. We simply didn't have the opportunity to challenge Mr. Sejdic -- sorry, Mr. Bobic's testimony here at that moment. But anyway, it was mentioned at the point. After that -- after that the Prosecution had of course the right to ask everything they wanted to Mr. Bobic when he was here. They had also the opportunity to tender his statement given to the OTP at that moment if they thought it would be a smart move for them, if they thought that this could support their case. They didn't do that. In our pre-Defence brief and in particular in our filing pursuant to Rule 71, under paragraph 15 there is a summary of Mr. Sejdic Naser and it was filed months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is -- this was the one filed on 14th November, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. And it says here he will testify on isolated incident which Mr. Zaric allegedly ordered the witness to arrest witness Bobic, Kemal. By using word "allegedly" it is obvious that we challenge that -- that piece of information. And we frankly express our concerns that this is a move from the Prosecution to tender into evidence some documents or evidence on a back door, since Mr. Bobic cannot now confirm anything in respect to that information. Mr. Bobic, while he was here - he was here for a couple of days here - and the Prosecution had the opportunity to ask him about this -- about all these facts, and they didn't do that. And now they want to tender it through another witness in -- I believe that this brings us into a very dangerous situation, that we could now make extracts of hundreds of statements, and whenever there is something that is different from the statement of one witness to another, to put this into evidence. And I believe that this is not the intention of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, why wasn't the statement put to the witness when he was giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's a misunderstanding here. I can answer that quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I mean Mr. Sejdic Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I did put it to him. I put it to him. It was the last question I asked. Do you remember when I said could I have leave? I put that portion to him and I said I suggest this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you did put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I put it to him. Mr. Lazarevic misunderstands. He never challenged the fact of the arrest. They were challenging that Zaric said to Sejdic, "Arrest Bobic." We had no indication ever that they were challenging the fact that Sejdic arrests Bobic. It's a complete misunderstanding. The cross-examination only goes to whether Zaric said it to Sejdic, and even then doesn't suggest that Sejdic never said that. And what my friend just read to the Trial Chamber allegedly said there is no indication until the witness got in the box that he was challenging the fact that -- he was saying that someone else had arrested Bobic. Two witnesses gave unchallenged evidence that Sejdic arrested him. We had no reason at the time to think that there was any challenge to it because it was never challenged, not in the Rule 71 filing, not in cross-examination, not till he actually got in the box. That's my point. We -- that's where it goes to credibility. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is fine, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They had that statement of Mr. Bobic in which he said well in advance Mr. Sejdic arrested me. That's in his statement. The Defence has had that statement for years and the portion in -- the previous portion, which I wish to tender into evidence - I'll be finished in a second - in which it says "on the 17th Sejdic told me that Zaric had said something." They were on notice for a long time that Sejdic was the person who arrested Bobic and that Sejdic had said to Bobic, "Zaric has -- Zaric told you -- gave me certain orders." There's no surprise about this. It was just not challenged. So we didn't lead it from the witness in re-examination. There's no back-dooring here. That's an absurd suggestion. Rule 90(H)(ii) is very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And if I can reply very briefly. The fact who arrested Kemal Bobic was absolutely of none interest for the Defence of Simo Zaric. We have, of course, never challenged the fact that Mr. Bobic was arrested, and at the point we really -- it was not of the interest for Mr. Zaric's Defence whether he was arrested by this, this or a third person. It was none of our interest. Then suddenly during trial a piece of information appears that it was allegedly ordered by Mr. Zaric. Of course we -- we didn't want it -- want to challenge anything related to harassment of Mr. Bobic, but then we were surprised by hearing here that it was allegedly ordered by Mr. Zaric. We are not defending here Mr. Sejdic. Why would we -- why would we challenge that at that point? But then when Mr. Bobic gave this piece of information that Mr. Zaric allegedly ordered Mr. Sejdic, this is the moment that we approached Mr. Sejdic. We didn't have the intention to bring Mr. Sejdic here. It was not of any interest for our case. When we approached Mr. Sejdic it was for the first time when we heard this information that actually he never arrested Mr. Bobic, and this is -- this is the position of Mr. Zaric's Defence. It wasn't whether he arrested or not Mr. Bobic. It was not of any interest of us until the moment when before this Trial Chamber Mr. Bobic said that it was allegedly ordered by Mr. Zaric. Why would we -- why would we be interested in that, whether it was Sole or Mr. Sejdic or some third person who arrested Mr. Bobic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think you've finished the question and you're now repeating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will give its ruling in due course. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not this particular topic. I wanted to raise another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we have a bit of time, I would like to raise a subject now which I believe would be in the interest of the further course of our proceedings. This is a subject that I must admit I've found troublesome for quite some time now. And now since we have time and because of the questions that were raised today, this has only corroborated my cause for concern. And this is what it's all the about, Your Honours: The Prosecution from the very beginning of the Defence case - I'm talking about the Defence case of Blagoje Simic too - during the cross-examination they often put the following questions: Do you have any reason to doubt the statement, et cetera, et cetera. And this relates to two types of evidence. One is the interviews of Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic respectively that are often put to witnesses partially, and others are admissions that appeared before this Court, Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Milan Simic, and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. Although at the very outset when the Prosecution started putting such questions the Trial Chamber admitted such questions, I believe that such questions and the answers that are obtained on the basis of such questions cannot be helpful to the Trial Chamber, regardless of the type of answer that is received from the witness. On the other hand, in this kind of situation, the Defence at that point in time is not in a position to question the type of answer that is given by the witness at that point. I am going to distinguish between the two. In relation to the interviews of Mr. Zaric and Mr. Tadic - and you will remember that questions were often put in this connection, and witnesses usually gave two types of answers - these interviews are very big, they're long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, following what you are saying, these are matters you'd put in your submissions regarding the weight that should -- the Trial Chamber should put to the evidence, not at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quite aware of that, that this was something that should particularly be analysed in final briefs. However, I think that especially with regard to these sections that are presented from various judgments, the Defence is not in a good position. Through the re-examination, it cannot put proper questions. Could I please explain why we cannot put proper questions? If you think that through a special submission we could express our views on this, I would be in favour of that. But I think that this is important for our further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is these are matters for your closing arguments, as to how the Trial Chamber should treat the evidence they listed in this or that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The weight is one matter, the weight of the documents. I understand that full well. We are going to deal with that. But the other matter is the ability of the Defence to give the motives to these witnesses, why some people admitted to certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't think that should bother you. The Trial Chamber is very much aware that it cannot accept certain types of answers from witnesses, depending on the type of witness who's being asked. So that shouldn't bother you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm worried about such questions are put to the witnesses in the first place and that witnesses present their views on certain things they do not know about. The same goes for Mrs. Biljana Plavsic too. We do not have the terms of the plea bargain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, I've told you that these are matters for your closing arguments. You should -- you should be able to attack the evidence which is supporting the Prosecution case in any way you feel like and give your reasons. You cannot do it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully appreciate that. Your Honours, I have understood your instructions. And I would just like to refer to yet another topic: Since as of Monday we will be starting a new way of examination related to Rule 92 bis, I would just like to ask the Trial Chamber for their instructions. When we are the ones doing the examination-in-chief of these witnesses, does this pertain only to those sections of their evidence that were taken out by the Trial Chamber? And the second question is whether the Prosecution can only limit themselves to what the statements of these witnesses say? Since this is going to be our very first time to deal with this kind of issue, as of Monday, we need guidelines. This in addition has to do with Rule 90(H). So basically is the entire statement part of the examination-in-chief and then how does this relate to 92 bis? I mean, we would really appreciate it if we could get instructions with regard to all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. The statements admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis are already part of the evidence of the -- the evidence in chief of that particular witness. For the paragraphs that were struck out and where the Trial Chamber has allowed the witness -- has ruled that the witness should come and give viva voce evidence, the viva voce evidence will be limited to those matters raised in those paragraphs only. Because you'll notice that these paragraphs were discussing the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment or very, very related to the conducts -- to the conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. That is the reason why they could not be allowed into evidence. So the examination-in-chief will be limited only to those paragraphs, and that's why the timing is also limited. When it comes to -- of course the witness will be shown the statement so that he realises that his evidence is already on record. That is the practical side. When it comes to cross-examination, almost in all -- almost in all the statements the Trial Chamber has not limited the Prosecution to any area of cross-examination. It has only given them the time limit. There's only one statement where the Trial Chamber, I think, limited the cross-examination to events of the 16th and 17th. Yes, and there are reasons for that. Is that clear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite clear. Thank you very much for these instructions. This will be very valuable for preparing our witnesses. Thank you.

THE ACCUSED TADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have not given this any thought. THE ACCUSED ZARIC: [Interpretation] No, that would be far too strenuous for me, really, far too strenuous. As I am now, I think I am fully stretched in terms of health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just a very quick clarification. Ms. Winner -- sorry, our case manager has just drawn to my attention: Your Honour said there were four 92 bis statements from Mr. Pantelic that were outstanding. Was that --
